name: Adam
summary: The first man, formed by God from the dust of the ground and given the breath of life, placed in the garden of Eden to till and keep it. With Eve he disobeyed God's command by eating from the tree of the knowledge of good and evil, and they were driven from the garden. He fathered Cain, Abel and Seth, and lived 930 years.
catholic: St Paul calls Adam 'a type of him who was to come' (Rom 5:14): as sin and death entered through the first Adam's disobedience, grace and life come through Christ, the New Adam (1 Cor 15:22, 45). The Catechism treats man's creation in God's image, original justice, and the Fall at length (CCC 355-379, 385-421), teaching that Adam's sin is transmitted to all humanity as original sin (CCC 404) and that Christ is the new Adam (CCC 359, 504). The Exsultet at the Easter Vigil sings of the 'truly necessary sin of Adam' and the 'happy fault' that won so great a Redeemer. An ancient tradition placed Adam's grave at Golgotha, which is why a skull is often painted at the foot of the crucifix.

Named the animals and received Eve as a suitable helper (Gen 2:18-23)
His disobedience brought sin and death into the world (Rom 5:12)
Christ is called the 'last Adam' (1 Cor 15:45)
Father of Cain, Abel and Seth; lived 930 years (Gen 5:5)

name: Eve
summary: The first woman, built by God from the man's rib to be his partner. Deceived by the serpent, she ate the forbidden fruit and gave it to Adam; God announced enmity between the serpent and the woman's offspring. Adam named her Eve because she was 'the mother of all the living'; she bore Cain, Abel and Seth.
catholic: The Fathers contrast Eve with Mary, the New Eve: St Irenaeus wrote that 'the knot of Eve's disobedience was untied by Mary's obedience', and St Jerome 'death through Eve, life through Mary' (both quoted in CCC 494). Gen 3:15, the 'protoevangelium' or first announcement of the Gospel, is read by Christian tradition as foretelling the New Adam and the New Eve, Mary, who shares in his victory over sin (CCC 410-411). Mary is thus honoured as the true 'mother of the living' in the order of grace. The Catechism also names Eve among the women whose mission prepared for Mary's (CCC 489).

name: Cain
summary: The firstborn son of Adam and Eve, a tiller of the ground. When God accepted Abel's offering but not his, Cain in anger killed his brother in the field, then asked, 'Am I my brother's keeper?' God sent him away as a wanderer but put a mark on him so no one would kill him; he settled in the land of Nod and founded a city named after his son Enoch.
catholic: The Catechism presents Cain's murder of Abel as the first fruit of sin spreading after the Fall (CCC 401) and as Scripture's revelation of anger and envy at the root of violence against human life (CCC 2259). The New Testament holds him up as a warning: 1 John 3:12 says he 'was of the evil one', and Jude 11 warns against 'the way of Cain'. St Augustine's City of God makes Cain the founder of the earthly city built on self-love, in contrast to Abel the pilgrim of the city of God. God's protection of Cain is often cited as a sign that even the guilty keep their dignity.

name: Abel
summary: The second son of Adam and Eve, a keeper of sheep. He offered God the firstborn of his flock and their fat portions, and God looked with favour on his offering. His jealous brother Cain killed him, and his blood cried out to God from the ground.
catholic: Jesus calls him 'righteous Abel' (Mt 23:35), and Hebrews praises his faith-filled sacrifice and says Christ's blood 'speaks better than that of Abel' (Heb 11:4; 12:24). In the Roman Canon (Eucharistic Prayer I) the Church asks God to accept the Eucharistic offering as he accepted 'the gifts of your servant Abel the just', together with Abraham's sacrifice and Melchizedek's offering. He is seen as a type of Christ the innocent shepherd slain by his brother, and as the first martyr. The Catechism points to his offering of the firstborn of his flock as an early form of prayer (CCC 2569) and to his murder as revealing the evil of homicide (CCC 2259).

name: Seth
summary: The third son of Adam and Eve, born after Abel's death; Eve said God had given him 'instead of Abel'. Adam fathered him 'in his own likeness, after his image' at 130 years. He was the father of Enosh and lived 912 years; the line leading to Noah, Abraham and David runs through him.
catholic: Seth's line carries the promise after the tragedy of Cain and Abel, and Luke traces Jesus' genealogy back through Seth to Adam (Lk 3:38). St Augustine's City of God follows the 'city of God' through Seth's descendants, in contrast with Cain's line. Sirach 49:16 honours him with Shem.

The Catechism cites his 'walk with God' as a model of prayer (CCC 2569). Several Church Fathers expected Enoch, with Elijah, to return before the end as the two witnesses of Revelation 11, though this is not defined teaching. Jude 14-15 quotes a prophecy attributed to him.

name: Noah
summary: A righteous man, blameless in his generation, who 'walked with God'. When God resolved to send the Flood on a corrupt earth, he commanded Noah to build an ark and bring his family and the animals into it. After the waters receded, Noah built an altar, and God made a covenant with him and all living creatures, sealed by the rainbow. He planted a vineyard, became drunk, and cursed Canaan after Ham's disrespect; he lived 950 years.
catholic: The Catechism teaches that the covenant with Noah, God's covenant with all nations, 'remains in force during the times of the Gentiles' (CCC 56-58, 71), and counts Noah among the righteous of the nations (CCC 58). The ark is a classic figure of the Church, 'which alone saves from the flood' (CCC 845), and the Flood waters prefigure Baptism (CCC 1219; 1 Pt 3:20-21), as the Easter Vigil blessing of water recalls. His upright offering after the Flood is cited in the Catechism's history of prayer (CCC 2569). Jesus compares the days of Noah with the coming of the Son of Man (Mt 24:37-39).

catholic: Noah's blessing of the God of Shem points to the line through which God's promise passes to Abraham, Israel and Christ, whom Luke lists as 'son of Shem' (Lk 3:36). Sirach 49:16 says 'Shem and Seth were honoured among men'.

name: Abraham
summary: Called by God to leave his country and kindred for the land God would show him, Abram obeyed and received the promise that he would become a great nation and that all families of the earth would be blessed in him. God made a covenant with him, renamed him Abraham ('father of a multitude'), and in old age gave him Isaac by Sarah. When God tested him by commanding him to offer Isaac on Mount Moriah, he obeyed and God provided a ram instead; he died at 175 and was buried at Machpelah.
catholic: The Church honours Abraham as 'our father in faith', as the Roman Canon calls him, and the Catechism presents him as the model of the obedience of faith (CCC 144-146) and of believing prayer (CCC 2570-2572). God's call to him begins the gathering of the People of God (CCC 59-60, 762), and his willingness to offer Isaac conforms him to the Father 'who did not spare his own Son' (CCC 2572; Rom 8:32). St Paul makes him the father of all who believe, Jew and Gentile, justified by faith (Rom 4; Gal 3). Eastern tradition and Rublev's famous icon read the three visitors at Mamre (Gen 18) as a foreshadowing of the Trinity; the Roman Martyrology commemorates him on 9 October.

name: Sarah
summary: Wife and half-sister of Abraham, long barren. She gave her servant Hagar to Abraham, then resented her. God renamed her from Sarai to Sarah and promised her a son; she laughed at the promise but bore Isaac at ninety. She died at 127 in Hebron and was buried in the cave of Machpelah.
catholic: Hebrews praises Sarah's faith in receiving power to conceive (Heb 11:11), and 1 Peter holds her up as a model for Christian wives (1 Pt 3:6). St Paul makes her, the free woman, an image of the 'Jerusalem above' who is mother of believers (Gal 4:22-31). Her miraculous motherhood is among the Old Testament signs preparing for Mary's virginal motherhood (CCC 489). The traditional Roman nuptial blessing prayed that the bride be 'long-lived and faithful like Sarah'.

name: Hagar
summary: Sarah's Egyptian servant, given to Abraham as a wife so that Sarah might have children through her. After Isaac's birth she and her son Ishmael were sent away, and God saved them in the wilderness of Beersheba by opening her eyes to a well.

Yet Genesis shows God's tender care for her: she is the first person in Scripture visited by the angel of the LORD and the only one to give God a name, 'the God who sees' (Gen 16:13).

The Roman Canon asks God to accept the Eucharistic sacrifice as he accepted 'the offering of your high priest Melchizedek, a holy sacrifice, a spotless victim'. Psalm 110:4 is traditionally sung at priestly ordinations.

catholic: God's dream-warning to Abimelech, a foreign king who acts 'in the integrity of my heart' (Gen 20:5-6), shows God's providence protecting the promise and also the moral conscience of Gentiles.

name: Isaac
summary: The son of the promise, born to Abraham and Sarah in their old age and named 'laughter'. As a youth he was bound on the altar on Mount Moriah until God provided a ram. He married Rebekah, who bore the twins Esau and Jacob; in old age and blind, he was deceived into giving Jacob the blessing meant for Esau. He died at 180 and was buried by his sons.
catholic: The Church sees in the binding of Isaac (the Akedah) a figure of Christ's sacrifice: the beloved only son carries the wood up the mountain, is offered by his father, and is received back 'figuratively' from the dead (Heb 11:17-19); Fathers such as Origen compare Isaac carrying the wood to Christ carrying his Cross. The Catechism links Abraham's offering to the Father who 'did not spare his own Son' (CCC 2572). St Paul calls Christians 'children of promise, as Isaac was' (Gal 4:28). God is named 'the God of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob' (Ex 3:6), and Jesus uses this title to teach the resurrection (Mt 22:32).
know: Name means 'he laughs' (Gen 21:3-6)
Bound on Mount Moriah; God provided a ram (Gen 22)
Married Rebekah and loved her (Gen 24:67)
Father of the twins Esau and Jacob (Gen 25:24-26)
Blessed Jacob in place of Esau (Gen 27)

name: Rebekah
summary: Daughter of Bethuel, found at the well by Abraham's servant, whom she generously watered with his camels. She agreed to go and marry Isaac, and after twenty years of barrenness bore Esau and Jacob, receiving the oracle that 'the elder will serve the younger'. She helped Jacob obtain Isaac's blessing and then sent him to her brother Laban to escape Esau's anger.
catholic: St Paul cites the oracle given to Rebekah before the twins were born as a sign of God's free election (Rom 9:10-13). The story of her betrothal (Gen 24) has long been read as a model of providence in marriage; the traditional Roman nuptial blessing prayed that the bride be 'wise like Rebecca'. Some Fathers saw her, leaving home to go to an unseen bridegroom, as an image of the Church called to Christ.
know: Watered the servant's camels at the well (Gen 24:15-20)
Said 'I will go' and married Isaac (Gen 24:58)
Mother of Esau and Jacob (Gen 25:24-26)
Planned Jacob's taking of the blessing (Gen 27:5-17)
Buried at Machpelah (Gen 49:31)

Buried under the oak of Allon Bacuth (Gen 35:8)
Not Deborah the judge

catholic: Laban is remembered as a figure of craftiness overruled by God's providence; Judith recalls how God tested Jacob 'when he kept the sheep of Laban' (Jdt 8:26).

Twenty years later he ran to meet Jacob and embraced him, and he settled in Seir; he is the father of the Edomites.
catholic: Hebrews warns against being 'profane like Esau, who sold his birthright for one meal' (Heb 12:16-17), and St Paul cites 'Jacob I loved, but Esau I hated' (Rom 9:13; Mal 1:2-3) to show the freedom of God's election, a Semitic idiom of preference rather than a statement of personal damnation. His generous reconciliation with Jacob (Gen 33) is a striking picture of forgiveness.
know: Elder twin, also called Edom ('red') (Gen 25:25, 30)
Sold his birthright for stew (Gen 25:29-34)
Lost Isaac's blessing to Jacob (Gen 27)

Father of the Edomites; settled in Seir (Gen 36:8-9)

name: Jacob
summary: The younger twin of Isaac and Rebekah, who bought Esau's birthright and, with his mother's help, received Isaac's blessing. Fleeing to Laban, he dreamed at Bethel of a ladder reaching to heaven and received God's promise. He served Laban twenty years, married Leah and Rachel, and fathered twelve sons and a daughter. Returning, he wrestled with a mysterious man at Peniel and was renamed Israel; he went down to Egypt in old age, blessed his sons, and died there at 147.
catholic: Jesus applies Jacob's ladder to himself: 'you will see heaven opened, and the angels of God ascending and descending on the Son of Man' (Jn 1:51), making Christ the true meeting-place of heaven and earth. The Catechism says the Church's tradition has retained Jacob's night-long wrestling as a symbol of prayer as a battle of faith and the triumph of perseverance (CCC 2573). His words at Bethel, 'This is none other than God's house, and this is the gate of heaven' (Gen 28:17), are used in the liturgy for the dedication of a church. From his twelve sons come the twelve tribes, which the Church sees fulfilled in the twelve apostles and the new Israel.
know: Took Esau's birthright and blessing (Gen 25:29-34; 27)
Dreamed of the ladder at Bethel (Gen 28:10-22)
Married Leah and Rachel; father of the twelve tribes
Wrestled with God and was renamed Israel (Gen 32:22-32)
Jesus is the true 'Jacob's ladder' (Jn 1:51)

name: Leah
summary: Laban's elder daughter, with 'weak' or tender eyes, given to Jacob in place of Rachel on the wedding night. Less loved than her sister, she was blessed with children: Reuben, Simeon, Levi, Judah, Issachar, Zebulun and Dinah, and through her servant Zilpah, Gad and Asher. She was buried at Machpelah beside Jacob's fathers.
catholic: Leah, the unloved wife whom God regarded (Gen 29:31), became the mother of Levi, the priestly tribe, and of Judah, the royal tribe from which Christ was born. With Rachel she is invoked in the blessing on Ruth's marriage as one of the two 'who built the house of Israel' (Ru 4:11), words long echoed in Christian marriage blessings.
know: Elder daughter of Laban (Gen 29:16)
Married to Jacob by Laban's trick (Gen 29:23-25)
Mother of six sons and Dinah, including Levi and Judah
Named Judah saying 'I will praise the LORD' (Gen 29:35)
Buried at Machpelah (Gen 49:31)

name: Rachel
summary: Laban's younger daughter, beautiful and beloved by Jacob, who served fourteen years for her. Long barren, she gave him her servant Bilhah, then bore Joseph. She stole her father's household idols when the family fled. She died giving birth to Benjamin on the road to Ephrath (Bethlehem) and was buried there.
catholic: Jeremiah pictures Rachel weeping for her children going into exile (Jer 31:15), and Matthew applies the verse to the massacre of the Holy Innocents at Bethlehem (Mt 2:18), read on their feast (28 December). Her long barrenness and joyful motherhood make her one of the Old Testament mothers whose children came by God's gift. The traditional Roman nuptial blessing prayed that the bride be 'loving to her husband like Rachel'.
know: Jacob served fourteen years for her (Gen 29:18-30)
Mother of Joseph and Benjamin
Took Laban's household gods (Gen 31:19)
Died giving birth to Benjamin near Bethlehem (Gen 35:16-20)
'Rachel weeping for her children' (Jer 31:15; Mt 2:18)

name: Zilpah

know: Mother of Gad and Asher (Gen 30:9-13)

name: Reuben
summary: Jacob's firstborn, by Leah. He lay with his father's concubine Bilhah, and so lost the pre-eminence of the firstborn. When his brothers plotted against Joseph he persuaded them to throw him into a pit instead of killing him, meaning to rescue him, and later offered his own sons as surety for Benjamin.
catholic: Reuben's instability ('boiling over like water', Gen 49:4) costs him the birthright, which 1 Chronicles says passed to Joseph's sons while leadership went to Judah (1 Ch 5:1-2) — a recurring biblical pattern in which God's choice does not follow birth order.
know: Firstborn of Jacob and Leah (Gen 29:32)
Lay with Bilhah and lost his birthright (Gen 35:22; 49:3-4)
Tried to save Joseph from the pit (Gen 37:21-22, 29)
Pledged his sons for Benjamin's safety (Gen 42:37)

name: Simeon
summary: Second son of Jacob and Leah. With Levi he avenged the violation of their sister Dinah by massacring the men of Shechem, which Jacob condemned. Joseph later kept him bound in Egypt as a hostage until the brothers returned with Benjamin.
catholic: Jacob's deathbed words curse the anger of Simeon and Levi (Gen 49:5-7), while Judith later prays to 'the Lord God of my father Simeon' and recalls his zeal (Jdt 9:2) — two readings within Scripture of the same violent act.
know: Second son of Jacob and Leah (Gen 29:33)
With Levi, killed the men of Shechem (Gen 34:25)
Held as hostage in Egypt (Gen 42:24)
Jacob rebuked his violence (Gen 49:5-7)

name: Levi
role: Son of Jacob; ancestor of the priestly tribe
summary: Third son of Jacob and Leah, whose name Leah linked to her hope that Jacob would be 'joined' to her. With Simeon he slaughtered the men of Shechem. His sons Gershon, Kohath and Merari head the Levitical clans; Moses, Aaron and Miriam descend from him through Kohath.
catholic: Though Jacob rebuked Levi's anger (Gen 49:5-7), his descendants were consecrated to the service of the sanctuary, and Aaron's line became the priesthood of the Old Covenant. Hebrews argues that Levi, 'in the loins of his father' Abraham, paid tithes to Melchizedek, showing that Christ's priesthood after Melchizedek's order surpasses the Levitical one (Heb 7:9-11). The Levitical priesthood is seen as a preparation for the ordained priesthood of the New Covenant (CCC 1539-1541).
know: Third son of Jacob and Leah (Gen 29:34)
Avenged Dinah with Simeon (Gen 34:25)
Father of Gershon, Kohath and Merari (Gen 46:11)
Ancestor of Moses, Aaron and the priests
Paid tithes to Melchizedek 'in Abraham' (Heb 7:9-10)

name: Judah
role: Son of Jacob; ancestor of the royal tribe
summary: Fourth son of Jacob and Leah. He proposed selling Joseph rather than killing him; later he fathered Perez and Zerah by his daughter-in-law Tamar, admitting 'She is more righteous than I.' In Egypt he offered himself as a slave in Benjamin's place, moving Joseph to reveal himself. Jacob blessed him as a lion from whom 'the sceptre will not depart'.
catholic: Jacob's blessing, 'The sceptre will not depart from Judah... until he comes to whom it belongs; to him will the obedience of the peoples be' (Gen 49:10), has been read by Jewish and Christian tradition as messianic, fulfilled in Christ the Son of David. 'It is evident that our Lord has sprung out of Judah' (Heb 7:14), and Christ is 'the Lion of the tribe of Judah' (Rev 5:5). Judah's transformation, from selling Joseph to offering his life for Benjamin, is a powerful example of repentance and substitution.
know: Fourth son of Jacob and Leah; name linked to 'praise' (Gen 29:35)
Proposed selling Joseph (Gen 37:26-27)
Father of Perez and Zerah by Tamar (Gen 38)
Offered himself in Benjamin's place (Gen 44:18-34)
'The sceptre will not depart from Judah' (Gen 49:10)

name: Dan
summary: Jacob's son by Rachel's servant Bilhah; Rachel named him saying 'God has judged me'. Jacob's blessing calls him a judge of his people and a serpent by the way.
catholic: Jacob interrupts his blessing of Dan with the prayer 'I have waited for your salvation, LORD' (Gen 49:18). Dan is the one tribe missing from the list of the sealed in Rev 7:5-8, which some Fathers connected with Gen 49:17; this is speculation, not Church teaching.
know: Son of Jacob and Bilhah; name means 'he judged' (Gen 30:6)
Father of Hushim (Gen 46:23)
'Dan will judge his people' (Gen 49:16)

summary: Jacob's second son by Bilhah, named by Rachel from her 'wrestlings' with her sister. Jacob calls him 'a doe set free'.

name: Joseph
role: Son of Jacob; ruler of Egypt
summary: Rachel's firstborn and Jacob's favourite, given a special coat and dreams of his family bowing to him. His jealous brothers sold him to traders, and in Egypt he served Potiphar, was falsely accused by Potiphar's wife and imprisoned, and interpreted the dreams of Pharaoh's officials and of Pharaoh himself. Made governor of Egypt, he stored grain against famine, tested and then forgave his brothers, and brought Jacob's whole family to Egypt; he died at 110 asking that his bones be carried to Canaan.
catholic: The Fathers saw Joseph as one of the clearest types of Christ: the beloved son, rejected and sold by his brothers for silver, humiliated and then exalted, who forgives those who wronged him and saves them from death. The Catechism quotes his words to his brothers, 'It was not you who sent me here, but God... you meant evil against me, but God meant it for good', to show how God's providence draws good even from evil (CCC 312; Gen 45:8; 50:20). Pharaoh's command 'Go to Joseph' (Gen 41:55) was applied to St Joseph, and Pope Leo XIII's encyclical Quamquam pluries (1889) compares the patriarch, guardian of Egypt's grain, with the guardian of the Holy Family. Sirach praises him: 'nor was there a man born like Joseph' (Sir 49:15).
